Filter out groups whose rewards are all equal and keep sampling until the batch has enough informative groups (dynamic sampling), or add harder prompts
Lower the learning rate
Divide advantages by the response length
explain: All-correct groups have zero advantage and contribute no gradient, so 60% of your rollouts are wasted. Dynamic sampling refills the batch with mixed-outcome groups; a harder curriculum attacks the cause.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Joining realtime to the schedule and propagating delay
question: A consumer joins TripUpdates to the schedule using only trip_id. For a daily train with trip_id N8 departing 20:00, the producer sends an update for yesterday's N8, now running 14 hours late. What breaks?
options: Nothing, delays over 12 hours are discarded by protobuf
The feed is rejected because delay must be under 3600 s
The update cannot be applied because it has no stop_id
The update is applied to today's N8, so riders see a wrong prediction
explain: Without start_date the consumer cannot tell yesterday's instance from today's. The reference requires start_date exactly when such collisions are possible. Always key realtime state by (trip_id, start_date) and, for frequency trips, start_time.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
question: You need an accurate L1 miss ratio, but you also asked perf for 10 other events, and every line shows about (40%). What is the best fix?
options: Run longer, since scaling error always averages out
Multiply both counts by 2.5 yourself
Put the two L1 events in one group with braces, or measure them in a run of their own
Switch to sampling mode with perf record
explain: Grouped events are scheduled together, so both counts cover the same instructions and their ratio is valid even if the group is multiplexed. Running longer does not fix phase-dependent bias, and scaling by hand is what perf already does.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a 2 MiB mapping: offset bits, alignment, contiguity
question: A server with 40 GiB of free memory runs `echo 10000 > /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages` (2 MiB pages, 19.5 GiB) and the pool only reaches 3,100 pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: nr_hugepages is capped at 3,100 by default
Huge pages count against swap, which is full
Free memory is fragmented, so few aligned 2 MiB runs of free frames exist
The kernel only allows huge pages up to 10% of RAM
explain: Allocation success depends on physically contiguous memory at the time of the request, as the hugetlb docs state. Retrying after compaction or allocating at boot (hugepages=N) works better. There is no default cap of that kind, and hugetlb pages are not swappable at all.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Why a fixed-size state forgets and a KV cache does not
question: A pure SSM answers a phone-book query with 555-284-7710 when the true number is 555-284-7719. What does this suggest?
options: The entry was compressed into the fixed state but cannot be read back exactly
The model never saw the entry, so it guessed a random number
The tokenizer split the digits incorrectly
The model needs positional embeddings to count digits
explain: Waleffe et al. found SSM answers share many digits with the correct number: information about each entry is in the state, but crosstalk from everything else blurs it. That is the capacity limit of a fixed-size memory, not missing information.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
question: In the Mamba-2 ablation, why is 24 of 48 attention layers worse than 6, beyond just costing more memory?
options: Attention layers cannot be trained with Mamba-2 layers
Too many attention layers cause the SSM state to overflow
Perplexity itself got worse (8.50 vs 8.26) at the same parameter count, so the extra attention displaced more useful SSM layers
The model ran out of position embeddings
explain: At fixed parameters, every attention layer replaces an SSM layer. The paper measured quality peaking near 10% attention, so going to 50% both raised perplexity and multiplied the KV cache by 4 compared with 6 layers.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Choosing a fusion method and running it at scale
question: You have 300 labeled queries from your domain and two retrievers. Based on Bruch et al., which fusion is the better starting point?
options: A convex combination with alpha tuned on the labeled queries
RRF with k = 60, because it never needs tuning
Raw score sum, since labels make normalization unnecessary
Whichever retriever is better alone, without fusion
explain: Their study found a tuned convex combination outperformed RRF in and out of domain, and that a small labeled set suffices to tune alpha. RRF remains a good zero-shot default when you have no labels.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: Users of an internal tool type short product code names that the LLM has never seen. HyDE with N=8 is underperforming plain dense retrieval. What is the best first change?
options: Give the raw query far more weight, or skip HyDE for these queries: every sample shares the same misreading, so averaging cannot fix it
Raise N to 32 so the noise averages out
Raise the temperature for more diverse passages
Switch the encoder for the hypothetical passages only
explain: Unfamiliar names produce a shared bias, which more samples cannot remove (lesson 3), and N=8 even shrinks the query's weight to 1/9. Routing these queries to plain or lexical retrieval, or weighting the query up, addresses the cause. Switching encoders breaks the shared embedding space.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: If every pixel value in D were doubled (D' = 2D), how would Otsu's threshold and mask change?
options: The threshold doubles and the mask stays the same
The threshold stays the same and the mask doubles in size
Both stay the same
The threshold quadruples because variance scales with the square
explain: Scaling all values by 2 multiplies every class mean by 2 and every variance by 4, so the ranking of splits is unchanged: the same pixels are separated, at a threshold value twice as large. The variance scales by 4, but the threshold is a pixel value, not a variance.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
question: A helper function declares `char buf[4096]` locally, prepares an `IORING_OP_READ` into it, calls `io_uring_submit`, and returns. The caller later waits for the CQE. What happens?
options: Safe: the kernel copied the SQE at submit time, buffer included
The submit fails with -EFAULT because stack buffers are rejected
Safe as long as the read hits the page cache
Undefined behaviour: the read may complete after the function returned and write into a dead stack frame
explain: The kernel copies the SQE, not the buffer it points to. If the read does not complete inline it finishes later and writes into memory that may now hold another function's locals. Even the page-cache case is not guaranteed to complete inline. Keep buffers alive until their CQE arrives.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
question: A loop does `p = malloc(48); free(p);` a billion times on one thread. Without `local_free` (frees pushed straight onto `free`), what would mimalloc lose?
options: The guarantee that the slow path runs regularly, so remote frees and deferred work could wait forever
Correctness: blocks would be handed out twice
Locality, because blocks would come from other pages
Nothing; local_free exists only for debugging
explain: With one list, the same block is pushed and popped forever and free never empties, so malloc_generic never runs. thread_free would never be collected and deferred-free callbacks would never fire. local_free makes free run dry after a bounded number of allocations.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: A test with 5 client processes runs for 10 minutes and 40 writes end as info. Roughly how many operations can be concurrent near the end of the history?
options: At most 5, because there are only 5 processes
Exactly 40, the info writes alone
Zero, because the test is over
Up to about 45: the 5 live processes plus 40 writes that might still take effect
explain: Each info write stays open until the end of the history, and the crashed processes were replaced by fresh ones that keep issuing operations. So concurrency near the end is the live processes plus every unresolved info op, which is what makes checking expensive.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
question: You add one more knob to the matmul kernel: a vector width with 3 legal values. Everything else is unchanged. What happens to the 6000-configuration space?
options: It grows by 3 configurations, to 6003
It triples, to 18000 configurations
It stays at 6000 because vector width is derived from BLOCK_K
It grows only if you also add shapes to the key
explain: Knobs combine multiplicatively: every existing configuration is now three configurations, one per vector width. This is why autotuning is a search problem rather than a loop over a list, and why pruning matters before you compile anything.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
question: Why do people benchmark packet I/O with 64 byte frames rather than 1500 byte frames?
options: Because they maximize packets per second, so fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, syscalls, metadata) dominate and are exposed
Because 64 byte frames are the most common size on real networks
Because NICs can only DMA 64 bytes at a time
Because larger frames do not fit in a 2 KiB packet buffer
explain: Throughput in bits is the same, but small frames mean the most packets per second, and most driver and stack costs are per packet, not per byte. That is the worst case a data plane must survive.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
question: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell option on, a thread calls spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read 16 times and then calls spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions once. How many SQ tail doorbell writes did those 16 submissions need?
options: 0, NVMe needs no doorbell
explain: With the option set, submission only builds commands in the SQ ring; the doorbell is rung inside the poll call, once for everything submitted since the last poll.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
question: Using the Triton tutorial's count, what is the softmax speedup bound for M = N = 4096?
options: About 2x
About 3x
About 4x
About 8x
explain: Naive: (5MN + 2M) + (3MN + 2M) = 8MN + 4M element accesses. Fused: 2MN. Ratio (8MN + 4M) / 2MN = 4.0005 for M = N = 4096.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
question: Your loss uses F.kl_div(log_q, log_p, log_target=True, reduction="mean") on a batch of 32 examples over 1000 classes, then multiplies by T squared. Compared with the intended loss, the soft term is:
options: 1000 times too small, because mean divides by every element, not by the batch size
Correct as written
32 times too large
Equal to the cross-entropy instead of KL
explain: With reduction="mean" PyTorch averages over all 32 x 1000 elements. The KL per example is a sum over classes, so the mathematically correct reduction is batchmean (sum divided by 32). The soft term ends up 1000 times smaller and the hard loss silently dominates.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
question: You double the batch size and halve the context length per request. What happens to the total KV cache?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It grows 4x
explain: Total cache is proportional to batch x tokens per sequence. $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so the cache is unchanged, though per-step attention work per sequence drops.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
question: Why can layer-wise loading start computing layer 0 before layers 1 to 31 of the cached KV have arrived?
options: Because attention at layer 0 only reads layer 0's keys and values
Because the GPU recomputes the missing layers in parallel
Because KV caches are stored layer-interleaved by token
Because the scheduler skips attention for cached tokens
explain: Each layer's attention uses only the K and V produced at that same layer. Layer 0 needs nothing from deeper layers, so it can run as soon as its own KV is in HBM while later layers are still in flight.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
question: Two events have Lamport timestamps L(x) = 5 and L(y) = 9. Which conclusion is valid?
options: x happened before y
y did not happen before x
x and y are concurrent
x happened about 4 ms before y
explain: If y happened before x, the Clock Condition would force L(y) < L(x), which is false. That is all you can conclude: x may have happened before y, or they may be concurrent. Lamport timestamps have no unit of time.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
question: The ColBERT paper reports that at re-ranking depth k = 10 the BERT-base cross-encoder needs about 180x more FLOPs than ColBERT, but at k = 1000 it needs 13,900x more. Why does the gap widen as k grows?
options: ColBERT skips most documents once k is large
The cross-encoder's cost grows with k (one transformer pass per document) while ColBERT's dominant cost, the single query encoding, does not
MaxSim becomes cheaper per document when k is large
BERT attention is quadratic in k
explain: The cross-encoder pays a full transformer pass over query plus document for each of the k candidates. ColBERT pays one query pass regardless of k, and the per-document MaxSim is tiny. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, not in k.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: ColPali: late interaction over page images
question: BiPali and ColPali use the same PaliGemma backbone and training data, yet score 58.8 and 81.3 on ViDoRe. What is the difference between them?
options: ColPali runs OCR on the page first
BiPali averages the patch vectors into one vector per page; ColPali keeps one vector per patch and scores with MaxSim
ColPali uses a larger language model
BiPali only sees the page title
explain: The paper builds the model step by step. BiPali mean-pools the language model's patch outputs into a single dense vector. ColPali keeps every patch vector and uses late interaction, which is the 22.5-point jump.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
question: Why does Coconut, like iCoT, reset the optimizer state when the training stage changes?
options: To free GPU memory used by the KV cache
Because the loss suddenly changes, and Adam-style moment estimates from the old stage can produce badly scaled updates
Because the vocabulary changes when <bot> and <eot> are added
To force the model to forget the language reasoning steps
explain: Each stage is effectively a new task: some text targets disappear and new latent slots appear. iCoT found that without resets the accuracy collapsed and did not recover. Coconut follows iCoT and resets at stage switches.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Error windows, exponential search and monotonic models
question: A leaf has min_err = -2,000 and max_err = +2,000, but 99% of its keys are predicted within 8 slots. Which search strategy is likely faster on average, and why?
options: Exponential search, because its cost follows the typical error (about 8) rather than the 4,001-slot worst case
Bounded binary search, because the window guarantees correctness
Neither: both cost log2 of the array size
Linear scan, because errors are small
explain: Bounded binary search over 4,001 slots needs about 12 probes for every key. Exponential search with an error of 8 needs about 1 + 2 log2(8) = 7. Since nearly all keys are close, the exponential strategy wins on average, which is the effect ALEX measured.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
question: What does learned sparse retrieval keep from BM25, and what does it replace?
options: Keeps the inverted index and dot-product style scoring, replaces hand-made term weights with learned ones that may include new terms
Keeps the dense embedding, replaces the ANN index
Keeps the BM25 formula, replaces the tokenizer
Keeps nothing; it is a re-ranker
explain: The index structure and term-at-a-time scoring stay. The weights now come from a transformer and can sit on vocabulary terms the text never used.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
question: Why must LTR training data be grouped by query rather than treated as one big table of rows?
options: Because gradient boosting needs equal-size groups
Because the model needs the query text as a feature
Because labels and metrics only compare documents for the same query, so pairs and NDCG must be formed within a group
Because rows from different queries have different numbers of features
explain: A label of 2 for one query is not comparable to a 2 for another. Pairwise losses only pair documents of the same query, and NDCG is computed per query and then averaged.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
question: Result Z was shown at a position with estimated propensity 0.2 and was clicked 30 times over the logged queries. What total IPS weight do those clicks contribute?
explain: Each click is weighted by 1 / 0.2 = 5, so 30 clicks count as 150. Clicks at rarely examined positions count more because they reveal relevance that is usually hidden.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
question: A model reads a long code file, then a new unrelated file starts. Which mechanism lets a Gated DeltaNet head discard the old file's associations within a few tokens?
options: The delta rule with $\beta_t=1$
L2 normalization of keys
A small $\alpha_t$ at the boundary
The short convolution
explain: The delta rule only edits the direction of the current key, one association per token, so it cannot clear thousands of stale associations quickly. A small $\alpha_t$ scales the whole state toward zero at once.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Measuring judge agreement: confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa
question: In the toy, every disagreement is exactly one grade apart. Which statistic best reflects that the judge is never wildly wrong?
options: Quadratic-weighted kappa or interval alpha
Unweighted Cohen's kappa
Raw accuracy
The number of pairs
explain: Weighted kappa and interval alpha charge disagreements by squared distance, so many off-by-one errors cost little (0.786 and 0.790 here) while unweighted kappa treats them as full misses (0.333). Report both: the unweighted one tells you how often grades match exactly.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
question: A metric correlates poorly with human ratings of single responses but orders five systems the same way humans do. How should you use it?
options: Use it to flag individual bad responses in production
Never use it for anything
Use it, with care, to compare whole systems on a test set, not to judge single outputs
Use it only on outputs shorter than the reference
explain: Novikova et al. found the same pattern: metrics are more reliable at the system level than at the segment level, because averaging over many outputs cancels some per-output errors.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
question: In the toy, 5 of 7 disagreements involve the tie label. Which change most directly targets that?
options: Hire annotators who never use ties
Write an explicit tie rule with examples, run a calibration round, then re-measure kappa on a fresh overlap sample
Drop all pairs that any annotator called a tie, then report kappa on the rest
Switch to a 1 to 10 scale
explain: The disagreement is about what a tie means, which is a guideline problem. Dropping ties after the fact inflates agreement and biases the win rate; forbidding ties forces random picks on truly equal pairs.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Classifier guards: Llama Guard and NeMo Guardrails rails
question: Your agent reads emails and calls a refund tool. In NeMo Guardrails terms, which rail type is the most direct place to check that a refund call's arguments are allowed?
options: Input rails
Dialog rails
Execution rails
Output rails
explain: Execution rails control tool calls, their arguments and their results. Input and output rails see the user message and final response, not the tool call itself.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
question: Why does selective batching split the batch for attention but not for the QKV projection?
options: Attention has no weights, so batching it gains nothing and it must be skipped
The QKV projection runs on the CPU
Splitting the projection would require padding, splitting attention does not
Each token's projection uses only that token's row, but attention must combine a token only with earlier tokens of its own request
explain: A linear layer computes each output row from one input row, so the request a row belongs to is irrelevant and all rows share one weight read. Attention mixes rows, and mixing rows from different requests would be wrong, so it needs the boundaries (and each request's own past keys and values).

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: How vLLM, SGLang and TensorRT-LLM put it together
question: Which statement about the three engines is accurate according to their documentation?
options: All three swap preempted KV caches to CPU memory by default
SGLang keeps every running request's full max_new_tokens reserved until it finishes
vLLM V1 runs prefill and decode in separate scheduler queues with separate budgets
TensorRT-LLM's default capacity policy never pauses a request once started, while vLLM V1 recomputes preempted requests
explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT is TensorRT-LLM's default and guarantees started requests are not paused; vLLM V1 recomputes by default and removed CPU swapping for preemption. SGLang counts running requests' remaining tokens at an estimated ratio rather than their full maximum, and vLLM V1 uses one unified token budget.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: Why does the Outlines index map FSM states, rather than generated prefixes, to allowed tokens?
options: Prefixes are too short to be useful keys
There are finitely many states, each summarizing all prefixes that lead to it, so the table can be built once ahead of time
States are faster to hash than strings
The model's logits depend only on the FSM state
explain: Possible prefixes are unbounded, but the FSM has a fixed number of states, and any two prefixes that reach the same state allow exactly the same continuations. That is what makes ahead-of-time indexing possible. The logits still depend on the full prefix.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Ambiguity, negation and graceful fallback
question: Which parse is correct for *backend people who know java (not javascript) in hamburg*?
options: skills: [java], skills_not: [javascript]
skills: [java, javascript], skills_not: []
skills: [], skills_not: [java, javascript]
skills: [java], skills_not: [], text: not javascript
explain: Java is required and JavaScript is excluded. Option two is the dropped-negation error that appears in the lesson 5 set. Putting the exclusion in text makes it a scored match, which would actually boost profiles that mention JavaScript.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: PRP all-pairs at k=100 issues how many prompts, counting both orders?
explain: k(k-1) = 100 x 99 = 9,900: every unordered pair (4,950) in both orders.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: RankZephyr is distilled into 7B from GPT-4 orderings. Which cost quantity does distillation change?
options: The number of windows per query
The input tokens per window
The compute per token, plus access to batching, caching and logits when self-hosted
The number of output tokens per window
explain: Calls and tokens follow from k, w, s and L. Distillation shrinks the model, so each token costs less compute, and hosting it yourself unlocks the serving levers.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: Which change most directly reduces the number of listwise calls for 100 candidates?
options: Shrinking the window from 20 to 10 at the same step of 10
Raising the step from 10 to 15 with w = 20 (overlap 5)
Running a second pass
Adding more few-shot examples
explain: Calls per pass are floor((M - w)/s) + 1. With s = 15: floor(80/15) + 1 = 6 instead of 9. The cost is a smaller overlap (only the best 5 passages are carried along), and since 15 does not divide 80, the last window covers ranks 6 to 25 and ranks 1 to 5 are never reranked. Shrinking w to 10 with s = 10 removes the overlap entirely, so passages could no longer travel between windows.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
question: Which workload is the best fit for a cascade rather than a router?
options: A voice assistant with a 300 ms latency budget
A chat product where most answers are long essays
A nightly batch that labels support tickets into 12 categories, where a wrong label is cheap to detect
Any workload, because cascades are always more accurate
explain: Short answers make the wasted weak call cheap, a batch job does not care about the extra latency, and an easy correctness check makes the scorer reliable. A tight latency budget punishes escalation, and long answers make the wasted weak generation expensive.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: ORB: binary descriptors compared with XOR and popcount
question: You switch a working SIFT pipeline to ORB but leave `cv.BFMatcher()` with its default arguments. What is the most likely result?
options: It works the same, since all descriptors are vectors
Matches are much worse, because the default L2 norm treats bit strings as numbers
It throws an error because ORB has no descriptors
It becomes faster and more accurate
explain: BFMatcher defaults to NORM_L2, which is right for SIFT. ORB descriptors are packed bits, and L2 on the byte values does not measure how many tests disagree. Pass cv.NORM_HAMMING.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
question: Why should `compare_exchange_weak` be used inside a loop?
options: It may fail spuriously even when the value matched, so the caller must be ready to retry
It is slower than the strong version and loops hide the cost
It never updates `expected`, so the loop must reload
It only works on x86
explain: cppreference: the weak form may act as if the comparison failed even when it succeeded, for example when a store-conditional loses its reservation. Inside a retry loop that is harmless, and on LL/SC machines it can be faster. It does update `expected` on failure.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
question: In the hazard pointer protocol, why must a reader re-read the shared pointer after publishing its hazard pointer?
options: To refresh the CPU cache
Because the node may have been removed and retired between the first load and the publication, and a scan that ran in between would not have seen the hazard
To implement the ABA tag
It is optional; publishing is enough
explain: Michael's condition is that the hazard pointer must have pointed to the node continuously from a time when the node was still reachable. Re-reading proves the node was still in the structure after the hazard became visible, so any later scan will see it.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
question: You parse 2,000 lines. The ground truth has 40 templates. Your parser emits 60 templates, of which 30 group their messages exactly as the ground truth does. What are RGA and PGA?
options: RGA = 40/60 = 0.67 and PGA = 1.0, because every ground-truth template was covered
explain: Recall divides the correct templates by the ground-truth count (30/40 = 0.75) and precision divides by what the parser produced (30/60 = 0.50). Their harmonic mean is 2 x 0.75 x 0.50 / 1.25 = 0.60. Emitting too many templates, which is what over-partitioning does, is punished by precision; merging templates is punished by recall.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
question: Under YaRN with alpha = 1 and beta = 32, a RoPE pair completes 50 full turns within the original training length. What happens to its frequency when you extend by s = 8?
options: It is unchanged
It is divided by 8
It is divided by about 4, halfway along the ramp
It is multiplied by 8 to compensate
explain: r = 50 > beta = 32, so gamma = 1 and h(theta) = theta. High-frequency pairs only carry relative position, which is already in distribution at any length.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
question: You convert a 12-layer model into a (1 x 12) looped model of the same width. Which statement is correct?
options: Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Parameters drop about 12x and per-token FLOPs stay about the same
Parameters stay the same and per-token FLOPs drop about 12x
Both stay the same because the unrolled graph is identical
explain: The looped model stores one block instead of twelve, so parameters drop about 12x. But each token still goes through twelve block applications, so FLOPs (and latency) are about the same. The unrolled graph has the same shape, but its weights are tied, which is exactly what removes the parameters.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
question: You must ship a small on-device model mainly for trivia-style factual QA with no retrieval. Memory is tight, latency matters. Is a looped model a good fit?
options: Yes: looping recovers the full accuracy of a 4x larger model on any task
Not really: closed-book QA depends on stored knowledge, which looping recovers poorly, and every loop adds latency
Yes: looping lowers latency because the weights stay in cache
No: looped models cannot be quantized
explain: Closed-book QA is the task group where looping closed the least of the gap (58% for k = 6) because it depends on capacity. Loops also add sequential compute. Looping shines on reasoning over context; adding retrieval (moving facts into the context) is the setting where a looped model does better.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
question: Why does NF4 put more of its 16 levels near zero than a uniform 4-bit integer grid does?
options: Because pretrained weights are roughly normal, so equal-probability bins are dense where most weights lie
Because zero-valued weights are pruned and need no levels
Because the GPU can only multiply by values close to zero
Because the adapters only change weights near zero
explain: NF4 is a quantile quantizer for a normal distribution: each of the 16 bins holds about the same share of weights. Since most weights cluster near zero, the levels cluster there too, which lowers average rounding error for normally distributed data.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
question: In WHP, the baseline model ranks Ron first and Hermione second, but the reinforced model, knowing the books better, ranks Hermione first. Only Hermione's logit rises under reinforcement. What does the generic-prediction formula do?
options: Pushes down both Ron and Hermione equally
Pushes down Hermione but leaves Ron as the top prediction
Leaves both unchanged because the ReLU blocks them
Removes both tokens from the vocabulary
explain: The formula only subtracts where the reinforced logit exceeds the baseline. Ron's logit did not rise, so it stays and remains the top prediction: the method reinforces a Harry Potter answer instead of removing it. The paper names this exact caveat, which is one reason it adds anchored-term translation.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Training a Matryoshka model: one loss per prefix, summed
question: In the toy batch at m = 2, the Matryoshka-style model's loss is about 0.462. Why that value?
options: Two of the three queries score their match and one negative almost equally, giving about ln 2 = 0.693 each; averaged over 3 rows that is 0.462
It is the full-size loss divided by 2 because m = 2
Each row contributes 0.462 because the scale is 20
It is a random number; losses at small prefixes are noise
explain: With two near-equal scores, softmax puts about half its probability on the correct document, and the cross-entropy is -ln(0.5) = 0.693. q1 and q2 each pay that, q3 pays about 0, so the batch mean is 2 x 0.693 / 3 = 0.462.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: p = 8 pipeline stages, m = 32 microbatches, interleaved with v = 4 chunks per device. What is the bubble as a fraction of ideal time?
explain: (p - 1) / (v m) = 7 / (4 x 32) = 7/128 = 5.5%. Without interleaving it would be 7/32 = 21.9%.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
question: Under jemalloc, which request wastes the largest fraction of its block?
options: 1,000 bytes
33 bytes
300 bytes
2,048 bytes
explain: 33 bytes rounds to the 48-byte class (16-byte spacing among small classes), wasting 31.25%. The manual's 20% bound holds for all but the smallest classes. 1,000 goes to 1,024 (2.3%), 300 to 320 (6.25%), and 2,048 is exactly a class (0%).

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
question: A colleague says: "Our lock-free queue misbehaves in release builds, so we will ship it compiled with optimizations off." Why does this not make it correct?
options: Debug builds use different atomics
It does: without optimization the compiler emits code in source order and the bug disappears
The CPU can still reorder memory operations, and the compiler still may perform some transformations
Optimization level only affects speed, never ordering
explain: Mara Bos lists this as a myth: disabling optimization does not disable every compiler transformation, and it does nothing about store buffers, pipelining or other CPU reordering. The fix is to use the right orderings.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: On x86-64, which of these Rust operations compiles to a different instruction than its Relaxed version?
options: x.load(SeqCst)
x.load(Acquire)
x.store(1, SeqCst)
x.store(1, Release)
explain: Only the SeqCst store changes: it becomes xchg so that it cannot be delayed past later loads. SeqCst loads stay mov, because the cost is placed on the store side. Mixing the two possible conventions across compilers would break programs, which is why the mapping table recommends the store-side one.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
question:
Spot the bug:
`rcu_read_lock(); p = rcu_dereference(head.next); rcu_read_unlock(); x = p->data;`
options: rcu_dereference should be rcu_assign_pointer
rcu_read_lock cannot be called on head.next
There is no bug because readers never block
p->data is read after rcu_read_unlock, so a grace period may have ended and p may be freed
explain: Once the critical section ends, the reader no longer delays grace periods, so an updater's synchronize_rcu() can return and kfree(p). The kernel documentation shows exactly this pattern marked BUG. Read p->data before rcu_read_unlock(), or take a reference count to keep it longer.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
question: Your triplet loss drops to near zero within the first epoch, but retrieval quality barely improves. What is the most likely cause?
options: The margin is too large
The learning rate is too small
Triplets are sampled at random, so almost all are easy and give no gradient
The embedding is L2-normalized
explain: Random triplets are mostly easy: the negative is already beyond d(a,p) + m, so the loss is zero regardless of how good the embedding is. A low loss here says nothing. Mine harder triplets.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: DoNotOptimize, loop hoisting and who owns the loop
question: A Google Benchmark loop does `auto h = hash(key); benchmark::DoNotOptimize(h);` where key is a std::string built once before the loop. The result looks too fast. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add benchmark::ClobberMemory() after the hash
Call DoNotOptimize on key (or its data) inside the loop as well, so the hash cannot be hoisted
Wrap the call in your own loop of 1000 and divide by 1000
Run with --benchmark_repetitions=10
explain: The output is consumed, but the input never changes, so hash(key) is loop-invariant and may be computed once. Escaping the input each iteration forces recomputation. ClobberMemory only flushes pending stores; an inner loop gives the optimizer more to merge; repetitions repeat the same wrong number.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
question: A colleague sets rollout_batch_size 16, n_samples_per_prompt 4, global_batch_size 32 and num_steps_per_rollout 3. What happens?
options: Miles trains 3 steps and discards the 16 unused samples
Miles aborts with a validation error because 64 is not equal to 96
Miles reuses 32 samples to fill the third step
Miles silently changes n_samples_per_prompt to 6
explain: 16 x 4 = 64 samples are produced, but 32 x 3 = 96 would be consumed. With all four knobs set inconsistently, the docs say Miles aborts with a validation error instead of guessing which knob you meant.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
question: You train GLM-5 (744B) with 16 nodes per side and weight sync is eating about a minute per step. Which change matches the measurements in the docs?
options: Keep broadcast but double --update-weight-buffer-size; P2P only helps dense models
Use --colocate; the transfer then becomes P2P automatically
Switch to --update-weight-transfer-mode p2p; it cut GLM-5 updates from 58.3 s to 8.5 s
Switch to P2P only if you run on a single node
explain: The measured GLM-5 update fell 85.5% with P2P at 16 nodes per side. P2P's advantage grows with fleet width and is largest on MoE models, where expert parallelism cuts per-target data. On a single node it was slower. Colocated runs hand weights over locally, with no transport.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Decima: learning a cluster scheduler with reinforcement learning
question: Two training episodes use the same policy and the same actions early on, but in one a burst of 50 large jobs arrives at minute 5. What problem does this cause for policy gradient, and what fixes it?
options: The policy network runs out of memory; batch smaller
The reward becomes positive; clip it
The GNN cannot handle 50 DAGs; cap the number of jobs
Rewards differ for reasons unrelated to the action, inflating gradient variance; compare each episode against a baseline computed from episodes with the same arrival sequence
explain: The burst lowers every later reward regardless of what the agent did, so the advantage term blames or credits actions for luck. Decima's input-dependent baseline averages only over episodes that saw the same job arrivals, removing that noise from the comparison.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
question: Which property of matrix multiplication makes absorbing $W^{UK}$ into the query legal?
options: Commutativity: $AB = BA$
Associativity: $(AB)C = A(BC)$, so the up-projection can be grouped with the query instead of the latent
Distributivity over the softmax
Invertibility of $W^{UK}$
explain: Only regrouping is needed. Matrix products are not commutative in general, and $W^{UK}$ is not square (it maps 512 to 128 x 128), so it is not invertible. Lesson 4 shows how RoPE breaks this regrouping.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Merge, swap, or compute the adapter on the fly
question: Why can a merged LoRA model not serve requests for two different adapters in the same batch?
options: Because merged weights are stored in a different data type
Because merging removes the KV cache
Because the batch would need a different weight matrix for different rows, and a merged model has only one
Because the base model must be reloaded from disk for each adapter
explain: A matmul applies one weight matrix to every row of the batch. After merging, that matrix contains one specific adapter. Mixing adapters in a batch requires the shared W0 plus a per-row low-rank term, which is exactly the unmerged form.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Multi-LoRA in vLLM and LoRAX, and the cost model
question: Which statement about LoRAX matches its documentation?
options: It requires all adapters to be merged before serving
It only supports one adapter per GPU
It batches requests for different adapters together and swaps adapters between GPU and CPU memory
It replaces the base model with a quantized adapter
explain: LoRAX documents heterogeneous continuous batching (different adapters in one batch) and adapter exchange scheduling (prefetch and offload between GPU and CPU), using Punica's SGMV kernel.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: Users ask: "Which of our two vendors had more outages last quarter, and what did each change afterwards?" Retrieval misses half the evidence. What is the best fit?
options: Decompose into sub-questions (outages per vendor, changes per vendor) and retrieve for each
Multi-query with 6 paraphrases and RRF
Raise the RRF constant k
Use the unique union instead of RRF
explain: The question has several distinct parts. Paraphrases of the whole question keep mixing them; sub-questions target each needed fact, in the spirit of SubQuestionQueryEngine or Self-Ask.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines
question: With t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30 at 960 docs/s and the cheap reranker at 4100 docs/s, what is the largest k1 that fits a 150 ms budget in this model?
options: About 200
About 1000
About 125
About 400
explain: The precise stage costs 1000 x 30 / 960 = 31.25 ms. That leaves 150 - 20 - 31.25 = 98.75 ms for the cheap stage, which scores 4.1 docs per ms: 98.75 x 4.1 = 404.9 candidates.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Shared trunk, n heads, and the memory trick that keeps it cheap
question: In the paper's comparisons, a 4-token model and its next-token baseline have equal parameter counts. How?
options: The 4-token model uses a smaller vocabulary
The heads are linear layers with no parameters worth counting
Three layers are removed from the trunk to pay for the three extra head layers
The baseline is trained on four times fewer tokens
explain: Each head is one transformer layer. Adding n - 1 extra head layers and removing n - 1 trunk layers keeps the total equal, so gains cannot be explained by extra parameters.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
question: A layer has weight shape $16384 \times 4096$. Which part of Shampoo's state dominates memory and root-computation cost?
options: The right factor R, because it multiplies the inputs
The momentum buffer, because it is the same size as the weight
Both factors equally, since Shampoo is symmetric
The left factor L: it is 16384 x 16384 (268M entries) and its eigendecomposition costs on the order of 16384^3
explain: $L$ is $m \times m$ with $m = 16384$, so it has $2.7 \times 10^8$ entries versus $1.7 \times 10^7$ for $R$, and eigendecomposition scales as the cube of the side. This is why implementations block large dimensions, and why SOAP and its variants sometimes skip the larger side.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
question: With ZeRO-1, why does Distributed Muon need an extra collective that distributed AdamW does not?
options: Newton-Schulz needs the full momentum matrix, but each rank only holds a shard of it
Muon's momentum is stored in fp64 and must be broadcast
Muon recomputes gradients on every rank
Muon needs the Hessian, which is sharded across ranks
explain: AdamW's update is elementwise, so a rank can update its shard alone. Orthogonalization mixes all entries of the matrix, so Moonlight adds a bf16 DP gather of the momentum, runs Newton-Schulz on the full matrix and keeps only the local slice.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
question: A coord check of your muP Transformer shows the attention logits growing roughly like the square root of width after two steps, while every other curve is flat. What is the most likely bug?
options: Attention still divides q.k by sqrt(d_head) instead of d_head
The base width is too small
Weight decay is not scaled
The learning rate is too small for a coord check
explain: Once q and k become correlated during training, $q^\top k$ grows like $d$, so a $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale leaves logits growing like $\sqrt{d}$ times their target size as heads widen, while the rest of the network is fine. Switching to $1/d$ (or 8/d as in the README) fixes it.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
question: A thread calls lock on an unlocked three-state mutex and later unlocks it, with no other thread involved. How many system calls happen?
options: One: the wake in unlock
Two: a wait and a wake
One: the CAS is a system call
Zero
explain: The CAS turns 0 into 1 in user space. At unlock the swap returns 1, not 2, so the wake is skipped. Atomic instructions are not system calls; the kernel never sees an uncontended lock.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
question: Which change makes the doctors example safe while staying at Repeatable Read?
options: Run both transactions with a shorter timeout
Add an index on the on_call column
Lock the rows being counted, for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all on-call doctors, so the second transaction waits and then fails or sees the change
Switch to Read Committed so each statement sees fresh data
explain: Write skew comes from reads that do not conflict with the other transaction's write. Turning the reads into row locks (FOR UPDATE) materializes the conflict: the second transaction blocks, then hits a concurrent update error at Repeatable Read. Read Committed does not help; both counts can still run before either update.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
question: In the CoNLL-2003 data files, when does a B-ORG tag appear?
options: Only when an organisation starts immediately after another organisation ends
At the start of every organisation entity
On every token of a multi-token organisation except the first
Only on single-token organisations
explain: The files use IOB1, the Ramshaw and Marcus scheme: entity tokens are I-ORG by default, and B-ORG marks only the leftmost token of an organisation that immediately follows another organisation. The option saying every organisation entity starts with B-ORG describes IOB2, which is what most modern pipelines convert the files to.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
question: Your log tagger scores 91 F1 on a weakly labelled held-out split and 62 F1 on 200 hand-labelled lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weakly labelled split shares the labelling functions' blind spots, so it rewards reproducing them rather than finding entities
The hand-labelled set is too small for the metric to be meaningful
The model overfitted the 200 hand-labelled lines
Entity F1 is not comparable across splits
explain: A test set built by the same regexes and gazetteers as the training labels cannot reveal what those functions miss. The tagger gets credit for imitating them. Only human labels measure the task, which is why some of your annotation budget must be held out and never used for training.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Hardware alignment: the kernel and the measured speedups
question: Why does NSA's selection kernel loop over GQA groups at each query position, instead of tiling a block of consecutive queries like FlashAttention?
options: Consecutive queries can select different KV blocks, so a query tile would cause scattered, redundant loads, while heads of one group share exactly the same blocks
Triton cannot tile over the query dimension
It reduces the number of compressed tokens
It makes the selection differentiable
explain: Within a group, every head reads the same selected blocks, so each contiguous block load is reused h times. Consecutive positions have no such guarantee, so tiling them would not share loads.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Your service computes pHash with library X; a partner sends pHashes computed with library Y for the same images. Distances between matching pairs are around 30 of 64. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The partner's images were heavily edited
Hamming distance is undefined across libraries
pHash is random by design
Libraries differ in details such as resize filter, mean versus median and whether DC is included, so their bits are not comparable
explain: pHash is a family of variants. Krawetz uses a mean without DC, ImageHash a median with DC, and resampling filters differ too. Meta's PDQ documentation makes the same point: even one algorithm in different languages can give different hashes, so it defines conformance against the reference implementation.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: You write a custom environment that runs unit tests. It returns `rewards` as a dict `{"tests": ..., "style": ...}`. GDPO training fails to find the components. What is the most likely bug?
options: Environments may only return a single Tensor
The keys must use the reward/ prefix, for example reward/tests
Rewards must be Python lists, not tensors
Multi-reward environments must set terminateds to all zeros
explain: The environments guide states that each key of a multi-reward dict must use the reward/ prefix. The rollout then stores the summed total_reward and each named component for GDPO.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A program's working set fits entirely in each core's L1 and L2 caches. How much does NUMA placement of its data matter during the steady state?
options: A lot: every load must check the home node of the address first
It matters only for writes, since reads are always served locally
Very little: cache hits never leave the core, so the node only matters on misses
explain: Placement only changes the cost of requests that go out to DRAM. Hits in private caches are served inside the core no matter which node owns the page. NUMA effects show up when the working set misses the caches, or when cores on different sockets share written cache lines.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
question: A latency-bound service (pointer chasing, one outstanding miss at a time) runs one thread per node. Which placement is best for it?
options: Keep each thread's data on its own node
Interleave all memory, to use both controllers
Bind everything to node 0 for predictability
explain: With one outstanding miss at a time, bandwidth is not the limit; every miss pays the latency. Local placement gives f = 0, the lowest average latency. Interleave would make half the misses remote.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
question: Two drives have identical flash. Drive X exposes 960 GB from 1024 GB of flash, drive Y exposes 1000 GB. Under sustained random overwrites, which is true?
options: Same write amplification, since the flash is identical
Y has lower write amplification because it has more capacity to spread writes
X has higher amplification because GC runs more often
X has lower write amplification because more spare means emptier victims
explain: X has S_f = 64/1024, about 6.3%; Y has 24/1024, about 2.3%. Less spare means victims are fuller when cleaned, and A = 1/(1-u) rises steeply as u approaches 1.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: A people-counting deployment in a packed train station uses NMS at IoU 0.5 and consistently undercounts. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Raise the NMS IoU threshold (or use a detector that needs no NMS), because overlapping people are being suppressed as duplicates
Lower the NMS IoU threshold to 0.3
Raise the confidence threshold to remove false positives
Switch to xywh box format
explain: Undercounting in crowds is the signature of NMS deleting true boxes whose IoU with a neighbor exceeds the threshold. Lowering it to 0.3 would suppress even more. A higher threshold, or a set-prediction detector, keeps overlapping people. Raising the confidence threshold removes boxes, so it would lower the count further.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
question: Which S3 guarantee is what lets a brand-new node read a file that another node wrote a moment ago, without any coordination between the two nodes?
options: Eleven nines of durability
Strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs
Storage across at least 3 Availability Zones
Per-prefix request rate scaling
explain: Durability and multiple AZs keep data safe, but a reader could still see a stale or missing object if S3 were eventually consistent. Strong read-after-write consistency means any GET or LIST that starts after a successful PUT returns the new object, so a fresh node can trust what it reads.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
question: A team enables tiered storage and expects produce latency to drop because brokers now have less data on disk. What actually happens to produce latency?
options: It drops, since disks are less full
It rises to S3 PUT latency
It becomes unpredictable because acks wait for remote copies
It is essentially unchanged: produce still goes through the leader and in-sync replicas; remote copying happens later, for rolled segments only
explain: Tiering changes what happens to data after a segment rolls. The produce path, leader append plus replication to in-sync replicas, is the same as without tiering, so latency does not drop or rise because of it. The wins are smaller disks and faster broker replacement and rebalancing.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
question: A receipt pipeline reads every character correctly, yet it reports the subtotal as the total. Which stage most likely failed?
options: Layout analysis and field mapping: the right words were read but linked to the wrong field
Text detection: the total was never found
Recognition: the digits were misread
Binarization: the image was too dark
explain: If every character was read correctly, detection and recognition did their jobs. Picking the wrong number is a structure problem, which is exactly what the layout-aware models in lesson 5 address.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
question: In the tiny project, you edit ops.h. Which objects recompile?
options: Only add.o and matmul.o, since ops.h declares their functions
add.o, matmul.o and main.o
All 5 objects, because ops.h includes tensor.h
None until you run a clean build
explain: add.cpp, matmul.cpp and main.cpp include ops.h, so 3 of 5 objects recompile. The include edge tensor.h to ops.h points the other way: editing ops.h does not affect files that only include tensor.h, such as tensor.cpp.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
question: A CUDA-heavy project takes 90 minutes to build with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=all. You only need to test on your own CC 8.9 GPU. Which change cuts build time the most while still running locally?
options: Set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (or 89)
Switch the generator from Ninja to Makefiles
Set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
Use 89-virtual so the driver compiles at startup
explain: With all, every .cu file is compiled for every supported real architecture plus PTX; a single native target removes nearly all of that repeated device compilation. 89-virtual also builds once, but then every run JIT compiles all kernels at startup, which is slow for a large project.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
question: A maintainer proposes `--reruns 3` globally to fix red CI. Which concern is most serious?
options: Reruns make pytest exit with code 5
A real race condition that fails 50 percent of runs would be reported only $0.5^4 = 6.25$ percent of the time
Reruns are not supported on GitHub Actions
Reruns change the order tests are collected in
explain: With 3 reruns a test is reported failed only if all 4 attempts fail. For a real intermittent bug with $q = 0.5$, that is $0.5^4 = 0.0625$, so about 94 percent of runs would be green despite the bug.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Giving review: reading order and comments that land
question: Which comment is phrased the way this lesson recommends?
options: "You clearly didn't test this."
"Nit: this could be a list comprehension, but the loop is fine too."
"This is wrong."
"Why would anyone write it like this?"
explain: It is labeled (Nit: tells the author it is optional), it is about the code, and it says the existing version is acceptable. The others aim at the person or give no reason and no way forward.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
question: You find a way to read other users' files through a project's upload endpoint. The repo has SECURITY.md and private vulnerability reporting enabled. What do you do?
options: Use the private report (or the channel SECURITY.md names) and follow its instructions
Open a detailed public issue so the fix gets attention quickly
Open a PR with the fix and describe the exploit in the PR body
Post a minimal reproducer in the project's public chat
explain: Public issues, PRs and chat disclose the vulnerability before a fix ships. SECURITY.md gives the project's reporting instructions, and private vulnerability reporting delivers the report only to maintainers.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
question: Halfway through a rebase, Git stops with a conflict in `parser.c` and you are unsure of your fix. Which command returns the branch to exactly where it was before you started?
options: `git rebase --skip`
`git rebase --abort`
`git rebase --continue`
`git reset --hard upstream/main`
explain: `--abort` stops the rebase and restores the original branch. `--skip` drops the conflicting commit and keeps going, which loses that change. `--continue` needs the conflict resolved and staged. Resetting to upstream/main throws away all your commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
question: Your company uses an Apache-2.0 library and later files a patent suit claiming that library infringes one of its patents. What happens under section 3?
options: The patent licenses your company received for that library terminate as of the filing date
The copyright license terminates and you must stop using the code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 only covers copyright
The library's contributors lose their own patents
explain: Section 3 grants a patent license from each contributor, and it terminates for anyone who starts patent litigation alleging the Work infringes. The copyright license in section 2 is not what terminates.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
question: A project wants contributor provenance with minimal friction for drive-by contributors, and does not need any rights beyond its license. Which fits best?
options: A corporate CLA with each contributor's employer
The DCO with a sign-off check on every commit
An individual CLA signed before any PR is reviewed
No policy, since inbound=outbound needs no record at all
explain: The DCO adds one trailer per commit and no paperwork, while still recording a certification of origin. CLAs suit projects that want an explicit, signed grant (often including patents); no policy leaves no record of who certified the code's origin.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
question: Your search for a function name returns 40 hits, 30 of them under deps/. What is the best next step for a Redis server bug?
options: Read all 40 hits in order
Delete deps/ from your clone so search is faster
Search only the tests
Restrict the search to src, for example `git grep -n name -- src`, since deps is vendored third-party code
explain: Vendored code is a copy of another project. Bugs there are usually fixed upstream, not in this repo. A pathspec after `--` limits git grep to the directories that matter without changing the checkout.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
question: A maintainer replies "works for me" to your report. Which addition is most likely to turn it into a reproduction?
options: A longer description of how important the bug is to your team
The exact versions of the library, Python and OS you ran, plus the input that triggered it as text
A screenshot of the stack trace with the failing line circled
A link to your full private application repository
explain: "Works for me" usually means your environment or input differs from theirs in a way the report did not capture. Exact versions and the triggering input close that gap. A screenshot is not searchable, a private repo is not runnable by them, and urgency does not help them see the bug.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
question: Your repro fails on your GPU machine but passes on the maintainer's CPU-only laptop, even with `torch.manual_seed(0)`. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assume the maintainer made a mistake and ask them to retry
Remove the seed, since it obviously does not help
Report the device and the collect_env output, and check whether the failure needs the GPU path (for example, run your repro on CPU yourself)
explain: PyTorch's notes say results can differ between CPU and GPU even with identical seeds. Checking whether the failure needs the GPU narrows the hidden variable, and the environment report lets the maintainer match your setup.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
question: A request reserves 2048 contiguous slots and finishes after 300 tokens. What kind of waste are the 1748 untouched slots?
options: External fragmentation, because they sit between other requests
Internal fragmentation, because they are inside the request's own chunk and were never used
Reserved slots, because they will be used by later tokens of the same request
No waste, because the allocator frees them when the request ends
explain: They are inside the request's allocation and were never filled, which is internal fragmentation. The paper notes it is only known to be waste after the request finishes. Reserved slots are the ones that will eventually be filled; external fragmentation is space between allocations.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
question: You profile with `perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 10` on an 8-CPU machine where every CPU is busy. Roughly how many samples do you get?
explain: -F is per CPU and -a samples all CPUs: 99 x 10 s x 8 CPUs = 7920. 990 would be one CPU. 320,000 is what perf's 4000 Hz default would give on all 8 CPUs.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
question: You run `perf record -g ./server` as a normal user on a stock kernel and the flame graph has no kernel frames at all. Most likely reason?
options: perf_event_paranoid defaults to 2, which blocks kernel profiling without CAP_PERFMON
The server never makes system calls
-g only records kernel stacks when -F is given
Kernel frames are filtered by stackcollapse-perf.pl
explain: At paranoid level 2 an unprivileged user may profile their own user-space code but not the kernel. Run with CAP_PERFMON or root, or lower the sysctl on a machine you control.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
question: In an undo-log transaction, which ordering is required for correctness?
options: Modify the data in place, then write the undo entry, then fence
Make the undo entry durable, then modify the data in place
Invalidate the log, then flush the modified data
Flush the data only after the log has been invalidated, to save a fence
explain: Recovery can only roll back what the log holds. If the data change could become durable first, a crash leaves new data with no old copy. Invalidating the log is the commit point, so it must come after the data is durable.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
question: Which change can never shrink a C struct?
options: Moving the char fields to the end
Reordering fields so larger alignments come first
Moving a pointer field from the end to the front of a struct whose other fields are all pointers
Replacing an int field with a short when the values fit
explain: If every field is a pointer, every offset is already a multiple of 8 and there is no padding to remove, so moving one pointer changes nothing. The other options can each remove padding or bytes.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
question: Which change would most directly break the PAF score for a correct elbow-wrist pair?
options: Another person stands far away in the frame
The predicted field along the segment points sideways, across the forearm, instead of along it
The elbow heatmap peak is 0.6 instead of 0.9
The PAF predicts the wrist-to-elbow direction, and scoring uses the same convention
explain: The score is the dot product between the field and the segment direction. If the field along the segment points sideways, the dot products shrink. Distant people do not touch this segment, the peak height does not enter E, and a consistent direction convention is fine.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
question: Which query is the best fit for pre-filtering followed by a flat scan?
options: 50 million vectors, filter language = en matching 60% of them
2 million vectors, filter user_id = 42 matching 800 vectors
2 million vectors, no filter at all
50 million vectors, filter year > 2000 matching 90% of them
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching vector. 800 distances is trivial and exact. The other cases would scan millions of vectors, where a graph search touches only a small fraction.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
question: A core keeps 16 lines in flight and memory latency rises from 80 ns to 120 ns. Peak DRAM bandwidth is not the limit. What happens to this core's bandwidth?
options: It stays at 12.8 GB/s because peak bandwidth did not change
It drops to about 8.5 GB/s
It rises, because longer latency means more lines are in flight
It drops to 0.8 GB/s
explain: With concurrency capped at 16 lines, $B = 16 \times 64 / 120 \approx 8.53$ GB/s. Little's law says bandwidth is concurrency divided by latency, so longer latency at fixed concurrency means less bandwidth.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
question: A generator samples 100 solutions to a hard olympiad problem; 97 have wrong final answers. Why is outcome supervision on this problem a weak training signal for a reward model?
options: Outcome labels are noisy because the answer checker is usually wrong
Almost every label is 0, and a 0 does not say which step failed, so the model learns little about where reasoning breaks
Outcome labels cannot be computed for olympiad problems
The reward model would overfit to the 3 correct solutions and ignore the rest
explain: When nearly all solutions are wrong, a 0 is the expected label and says only 'some step was wrong'. Lightman et al. make exactly this credit-assignment argument: process labels also say how many leading steps were right and where the first mistake is.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
question: Which of these was NOT one of DeepSeek-R1's stated reasons for not using a PRM in large-scale RL?
options: Defining a fine-grained step in general reasoning is hard
Judging intermediate-step correctness is hard, and manual labels do not scale
A model-based PRM leads to reward hacking and retraining adds overhead
PRMs cannot rerank top-N responses or assist guided search
explain: DeepSeek-R1 says the opposite: PRMs show good ability to rerank top-N responses and assist guided search. Their objection was that the benefit in large-scale RL did not outweigh the extra compute and complexity.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
question: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than between two processes, even though both save and restore the same registers?
options: Threads have fewer registers
The address space stays loaded, so there is no page table switch, no TLB flush and the shared code and data may still be in cache
The kernel does not run the scheduler for threads
Thread switches happen entirely in user space on Linux
explain: With NPTL's 1:1 model the kernel schedules threads like any task, so the scheduler and register work are the same. The saving is the address space: no CR3 write, valid TLB entries, and shared data that may still be warm.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
question: An IVFPQ index with nlist = 1024 and PQ64 has poor recall. Profiling shows the true nearest neighbor is usually in the 3rd or 4th nearest list. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to PQ128 codes
Reduce nlist to 64 so lists are bigger
Turn off residual encoding
Increase nprobe from 1 to 8
explain: Neighbors in unprobed lists are never scored, so better codes cannot find them. Raising nprobe scans those lists. Shrinking nlist also captures them but scans a much larger fraction per probe; the paper finds that for a fixed fraction visited, more lists with more probes is more accurate.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
question: Your RAG program has a query-writer predictor and an answer predictor, but your data only labels final answers. How does BootstrapFewShot get demos for the query writer?
options: It cannot; you must hand-label good queries
It runs the whole program, and when the final answer passes the metric it keeps every predictor's input and output from that run as demos
It asks the proposer LLM to invent ideal queries without running the program
It fine-tunes the query writer on the answers
explain: Bootstrapping keeps full traces of runs that pass the metric, so intermediate steps get demos for free. That is the main reason DSPy needs labels only for the final output.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
question: Why does the many-to-one map from sequence to structure help a design pipeline?
options: It means each backbone has exactly one correct sequence, so the search is easy
It means structure prediction is impossible, so designs must be tested in the lab
It means many sequences fold to nearly the same backbone, so you can sample several per backbone and keep the ones that validate
It means the backbone can be ignored once the sequence is chosen
explain: Many sequences map to nearly the same fold. That redundancy is what makes sampling 8 (or 100) sequences per backbone and filtering them a sensible strategy, rather than needing to find the one true sequence.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: The funnel: from 100 backbones to a binder that works
question: Which statement about the two-stage pipeline is correct?
options: The backbone generator and the sequence designer are trained jointly, end to end, on experimental binding data
ProteinMPNN generates the backbone and RFdiffusion assigns the sequence
AlphaFold2 is used to generate candidate backbones, and RFdiffusion filters them
The backbone generator never sees a sequence, the sequence designer never changes the backbone, and a structure predictor is the referee between them
explain: The three models are trained separately and composed at inference. RFdiffusion places frames with no sequence, ProteinMPNN writes a sequence for fixed backbone coordinates, and AF2 or ESMFold judges whether the sequence folds back to the backbone. Nothing in the loop is trained on the assay results.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Expanding with models: doc2query, query2doc and HyDE
